Polity · STARTER CONTENT

Fundamental Rights · मौलिक अधिकार

Fundamental Rights protect individual liberty and place limits on state power. Part III of the Constitution makes these rights enforceable through courts.

मौलिक अधिकार व्यक्ति की स्वतंत्रता की रक्षा करते हैं और राज्य की शक्ति पर सीमाएँ लगाते हैं। संविधान के भाग III में दिए गए इन अधिकारों का न्यायालय द्वारा प्रवर्तन किया जा सकता है।

  • Articles 12–35 form Part III.

    भाग III में अनुच्छेद 12 से 35 शामिल हैं।

  • Article 14 guarantees equality before law and equal protection of laws.

    अनुच्छेद 14 विधि के समक्ष समता और विधियों के समान संरक्षण की गारंटी देता है।

  • Article 19 freedoms are subject to constitutionally permitted reasonable restrictions.

    अनुच्छेद 19 की स्वतंत्रताओं पर संविधान द्वारा अनुमत युक्तियुक्त प्रतिबंध लगाए जा सकते हैं।

  • Article 32 provides remedies for enforcement of Fundamental Rights.

    अनुच्छेद 32 मौलिक अधिकारों के प्रवर्तन के लिए उपचार प्रदान करता है।

Which Article provides the right to constitutional remedies?
  1. Article 14
  2. Article 19
  3. Article 32
  4. Article 44

Answer: Article 32

Article 32 guarantees the right to move the Supreme Court for enforcement of Fundamental Rights. Article 14 concerns equality, Article 19 certain freedoms, and Article 44 a Directive Principle.

Which of the following are included in Part III of the Constitution?
  1. Fundamental Duties
  2. Fundamental Rights
  3. Directive Principles
  4. Emergency provisions

Answer: Fundamental Rights

Part III covers Fundamental Rights. Duties are in Part IVA, Directive Principles in Part IV and emergency provisions in Part XVIII.

Polity · STARTER CONTENT

Parliament & its functions · संसद और उसके कार्य

Parliament consists of the President, the Council of States and the House of the People. It legislates, scrutinises the executive and controls public finances.

संसद में राष्ट्रपति, राज्यसभा और लोकसभा शामिल हैं। यह कानून बनाती है, कार्यपालिका की जवाबदेही सुनिश्चित करती है और सार्वजनिक वित्त पर नियंत्रण रखती है।

  • Article 79 defines Parliament.

    अनुच्छेद 79 संसद की संरचना बताता है।

  • A Money Bill can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha.

    धन विधेयक केवल लोकसभा में प्रस्तुत किया जा सकता है।

  • The Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha.

    मंत्रिपरिषद लोकसभा के प्रति सामूहिक रूप से उत्तरदायी होती है।

A Money Bill may be introduced in:
  1. Either House
  2. Rajya Sabha only
  3. Lok Sabha only
  4. A joint sitting

Answer: Lok Sabha only

A Money Bill can only be introduced in Lok Sabha, on the recommendation of the President. Rajya Sabha may make recommendations.

Parliament of India consists of:
  1. Lok Sabha alone
  2. Both Houses only
  3. President and both Houses
  4. Prime Minister and both Houses

Answer: President and both Houses

Article 79 establishes Parliament consisting of the President and the two Houses. The Prime Minister is not a separate constituent of Parliament.

Economy · STARTER CONTENT

Understanding inflation · मुद्रास्फीति को समझना

Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level. It reduces the purchasing power of money, though its impact differs across households.

मुद्रास्फीति सामान्य मूल्य स्तर में निरंतर वृद्धि है। इससे मुद्रा की क्रय शक्ति घटती है, लेकिन अलग-अलग परिवारों पर इसका प्रभाव अलग हो सकता है।

  • Demand-pull inflation follows excess aggregate demand.

    अतिरिक्त समग्र मांग से मांग-प्रेरित मुद्रास्फीति हो सकती है।

  • Cost-push inflation can follow rising input costs.

    उत्पादन लागत में वृद्धि से लागत-प्रेरित मुद्रास्फीति हो सकती है।

  • CPI measures changes in prices faced by consumers.

    उपभोक्ता मूल्य सूचकांक उपभोक्ताओं द्वारा चुकाई जाने वाली कीमतों में बदलाव मापता है।

A sustained increase in input costs may cause:
  1. Demand-pull inflation
  2. Cost-push inflation
  3. Deflation necessarily
  4. No price change necessarily

Answer: Cost-push inflation

Higher input costs can shift aggregate supply and raise prices. Demand-pull inflation instead originates in demand pressures; the other outcomes are not necessary.

If prices rise while nominal income stays constant, purchasing power generally:
  1. Rises
  2. Falls
  3. Remains unchanged
  4. Doubles

Answer: Falls

With unchanged nominal income, higher prices reduce the goods and services a household can buy.

Geography · STARTER CONTENT

The Indian monsoon · भारतीय मानसून

The monsoon is a seasonal reversal of winds. Differential heating, pressure patterns and the seasonal movement of the ITCZ shape rainfall in India.

मानसून पवनों की दिशा में मौसमी परिवर्तन है। स्थल और जल के असमान ताप, वायुदाब और अंतर-उष्णकटिबंधीय अभिसरण क्षेत्र का मौसमी स्थानांतरण भारत की वर्षा को प्रभावित करते हैं।

  • The southwest monsoon supplies most annual rainfall in India.

    भारत की अधिकांश वार्षिक वर्षा दक्षिण-पश्चिम मानसून से होती है।

  • Orographic uplift produces heavy rain on windward slopes.

    पर्वतों के पवनाभिमुख ढाल पर नम वायु के ऊपर उठने से अधिक वर्षा होती है।

  • El Niño can influence the monsoon but is not its only determinant.

    एल नीनो मानसून को प्रभावित कर सकता है, लेकिन यह अकेला निर्धारक नहीं है।

Heavy rainfall on windward mountain slopes is associated with:
  1. Orographic uplift
  2. Ocean salinity alone
  3. Earthquakes
  4. Tidal friction

Answer: Orographic uplift

Moist air rises over mountains, cools and condenses. The other processes do not explain orographic rainfall.

Which is the most accurate statement about El Niño and the Indian monsoon?
  1. It always causes drought
  2. It has no influence
  3. It can influence rainfall alongside other factors
  4. It always causes floods

Answer: It can influence rainfall alongside other factors

El Niño can weaken monsoon rainfall, but the relationship is not deterministic. Other oceanic and atmospheric factors matter.

Environment · STARTER CONTENT

Biodiversity & conservation · जैव विविधता और संरक्षण

Biodiversity includes genetic, species and ecosystem diversity. Conservation protects ecological processes and the services that support human life.

जैव विविधता में आनुवंशिक, प्रजातीय और पारिस्थितिक तंत्र की विविधता शामिल है। संरक्षण उन पारिस्थितिक प्रक्रियाओं और सेवाओं की रक्षा करता है जो मानव जीवन को सहारा देती हैं।

  • In-situ conservation protects species in natural habitats.

    स्वस्थाने संरक्षण प्राकृतिक आवास में प्रजातियों की रक्षा करता है।

  • Ex-situ conservation includes seed banks and botanical gardens.

    बाह्यस्थाने संरक्षण में बीज बैंक और वनस्पति उद्यान शामिल हैं।

  • Habitat fragmentation can isolate populations.

    आवास का विखंडन जीवों की आबादियों को अलग कर सकता है।

Which is an example of ex-situ conservation?
  1. National park
  2. Wildlife sanctuary
  3. Seed bank
  4. Biosphere reserve

Answer: Seed bank

A seed bank conserves genetic material outside its natural habitat. The other options conserve biodiversity in situ.

Biodiversity includes:
  1. Only species diversity
  2. Only genetic diversity
  3. Genetic, species and ecosystem diversity
  4. Only forest cover

Answer: Genetic, species and ecosystem diversity

Biodiversity spans variation within species, among species and across ecosystems. Forest cover alone does not capture these dimensions.

History · STARTER CONTENT

The Non-Cooperation Movement · असहयोग आंदोलन

Launched in 1920 under Gandhi, the movement mobilised people through non-violent non-cooperation with colonial institutions.

गांधीजी के नेतृत्व में 1920 में शुरू हुए असहयोग आंदोलन ने औपनिवेशिक संस्थाओं के साथ अहिंसक असहयोग के माध्यम से जनसमूह को संगठित किया।

  • It included boycotts of government schools, courts and foreign cloth.

    इसमें सरकारी विद्यालयों, न्यायालयों और विदेशी कपड़ों का बहिष्कार शामिल था।

  • Gandhi withdrew the movement after the Chauri Chaura incident in 1922.

    1922 की चौरी चौरा घटना के बाद गांधीजी ने आंदोलन वापस ले लिया।

  • The Khilafat issue helped broaden mobilisation.

    खिलाफत के मुद्दे ने जनभागीदारी बढ़ाने में भूमिका निभाई।

The Non-Cooperation Movement was withdrawn after:
  1. Jallianwala Bagh
  2. Chauri Chaura
  3. Dandi March
  4. Quit India

Answer: Chauri Chaura

The violent incident at Chauri Chaura in February 1922 led Gandhi to withdraw the movement. The other events relate to different moments.

Which was a feature of the Non-Cooperation Movement?
  1. Boycott of foreign cloth
  2. Armed rebellion as official policy
  3. Support for colonial courts
  4. Participation in all colonial institutions

Answer: Boycott of foreign cloth

Boycott of foreign cloth and colonial institutions was central. Non-violence was the stated approach.

Ethics · STARTER CONTENT

Integrity in public service · लोक सेवा में सत्यनिष्ठा

Integrity means consistency between values, decisions and actions. Public officials must put public interest before private advantage.

सत्यनिष्ठा का अर्थ मूल्यों, निर्णयों और कार्यों में संगति है। लोक सेवकों को निजी लाभ से ऊपर सार्वजनिक हित रखना चाहिए।

  • Accountability requires explaining and justifying decisions.

    जवाबदेही के लिए निर्णयों का स्पष्टीकरण और औचित्य देना आवश्यक है।

  • Conflicts of interest should be disclosed and managed.

    हितों के टकराव का खुलासा और उचित प्रबंधन होना चाहिए।

  • Legality and ethical conduct overlap but are not identical.

    वैधानिकता और नैतिक आचरण में संबंध है, लेकिन दोनों समान नहीं हैं।

An official facing a conflict of interest should first:
  1. Conceal it
  2. Disclose it through the appropriate process
  3. Ignore it
  4. Delegate secretly to a relative

Answer: Disclose it through the appropriate process

Disclosure allows transparent management of a conflict. Concealment or private arrangements undermine integrity.

CSAT · STARTER CONTENT

Ratios & proportions · अनुपात और समानुपात

A ratio compares two quantities. A proportion states that two ratios are equal. Keep units consistent before comparing.

अनुपात दो राशियों की तुलना करता है। समानुपात दर्शाता है कि दो अनुपात बराबर हैं। तुलना से पहले इकाइयों को समान रखना चाहिए।

  • For a:b = 2:3, the total is five equal parts.

    यदि a:b = 2:3 है, तो कुल पाँच समान भाग हैं।

  • Cross multiplication helps solve a/b = c/d.

    a/b = c/d हल करने में वज्र गुणन उपयोगी है।

  • Percentage change uses the original value as the denominator.

    प्रतिशत परिवर्तन में मूल मान को हर के रूप में लिया जाता है।

A sum of ₹500 is divided in the ratio 2:3. The larger share is:
  1. ₹100
  2. ₹200
  3. ₹250
  4. ₹300

Answer: ₹300

There are five parts. Each equals ₹100, so the larger share is 3 × ₹100 = ₹300.

A value rises from 80 to 100. Its percentage increase is:
  1. 20%
  2. 25%
  3. 80%
  4. 125%

Answer: 25%

The increase is 20. Dividing by the original value of 80 gives 25%, not 20%.

Historical Background · ऐतिहासिक पृष्ठभूमि

India's constitutional institutions developed through a long struggle over who could exercise public power and who could hold that power accountable. Colonial statutes are best studied as changes in control, representation and responsibility, rather than as a list of dates.

  • The Regulating Act, 1773 introduced parliamentary regulation of the Company's political affairs and a Governor-General of Bengal.

  • Pitt's India Act, 1784 distinguished commercial management from political oversight through the Board of Control.

  • The Charter Act, 1833 centralised legislative authority; the 1858 Act transferred government from the Company to the Crown.

  • The 1909 reforms introduced separate Muslim electorates; the 1919 Act introduced dyarchy in provinces.

  • The 1935 Act provided provincial autonomy and an envisaged federation that did not become operational as planned.

Making of the Constitution · संविधान का निर्माण

The Constituent Assembly transformed a negotiated transfer of power into a framework of popular sovereignty. Its legitimacy must be evaluated through both the limitations of its election and the depth of its deliberations.

  • The Cabinet Mission Plan, 1946 provided the framework for the Assembly; provincial representatives were indirectly elected by provincial legislative assemblies.

  • The Assembly first met on 9 December 1946. Rajendra Prasad became its permanent President.

  • The Drafting Committee was appointed on 29 August 1947 with B. R. Ambedkar as chairman.

  • The Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949; most provisions commenced on 26 January 1950.

  • Some provisions commenced immediately under Article 394. Adoption and general commencement are therefore distinct events.

Salient Features of the Constitution · संविधान की प्रमुख विशेषताएँ

The Constitution combines representative government, enforceable rights, social transformation and a division of powers. Borrowing an institutional idea from another system did not mean copying its entire political context.

  • A written, supreme Constitution limits both ordinary law and constitutional amendment.

  • Parliamentary government links the executive's continuance to confidence in the popularly elected House.

  • Federal distribution of legislative power coexists with a relatively strong Union and an integrated judicial system.

  • Fundamental Rights, Directive Principles and Fundamental Duties perform different legal functions.

  • Universal adult suffrage, an independent judiciary and judicial review help translate popular sovereignty into accountable government.

Preamble of the Constitution · संविधान की प्रस्तावना

The Preamble identifies the source of constitutional authority and the goals the constitutional order is intended to serve. Read each ideal as a relationship between citizens and public institutions, not only as a word to memorise.

  • Popular authority is expressed through We, the People; justice, liberty, equality and fraternity state interconnected goals.

  • Sovereign concerns independent authority; democratic concerns political participation and accountability; republic rejects hereditary headship of state.

  • The 42nd Amendment added Socialist and Secular and changed unity of the Nation to unity and integrity of the Nation.

  • Kesavananda Bharati (1973) recognised the Preamble as part of the Constitution.

  • It aids interpretation but is not an independent source of governmental power or an independently enforceable right.

The Preamble is best described as:
  1. An independent source of every executive power
  2. Part of the Constitution and an aid to interpretation
  3. A text that cannot be amended under any circumstances
  4. A replacement for Part III

Answer: Part of the Constitution and an aid to interpretation

The Preamble is part of the Constitution and guides interpretation. It is not an independent grant of all powers; amendments remain subject to basic structure; enforceable rights are specified elsewhere.

Union and its Territory · संघ और उसका राज्यक्षेत्र

The Constitution describes India as a Union of States while giving Parliament an important role in territorial reorganisation. Distinguish changes within India from admission of new territories and from cession to another country.

  • Article 1 describes India and its territory; Article 2 concerns admission or establishment of new states.

  • Article 3 allows formation of states and changes to areas, boundaries or names through the prescribed process.

  • A bill under Article 3 requires the President's recommendation; affected state legislatures receive an opportunity to express views within the specified period.

  • The affected state's consent is not constitutionally required merely because its views must be sought.

  • Article 4 treats specified consequential amendments under Articles 2 and 3 as outside the Article 368 amendment procedure.

  • The 100th Amendment relates to the India–Bangladesh land boundary settlement.

Mains prompt: Does state reorganisation illustrate flexibility or excessive centralisation in Indian federalism?

For a bill reorganising the boundaries of a state under Article 3, which statement is correct?
  1. The affected state must always consent
  2. The President must recommend introduction and the state is given an opportunity to express views
  3. A referendum in the state is invariably mandatory
  4. Every such change necessarily requires Article 368 ratification

Answer: The President must recommend introduction and the state is given an opportunity to express views

Article 3 requires the President’s recommendation and reference to affected state legislatures for their views within the specified period. Consent and a referendum are not mandatory merely under this provision; Article 4 covers specified consequential changes.

Citizenship · नागरिकता

Citizenship is a legal relationship linking a person to a political community. Residence, nationality, domicile, a visa and an OCI registration are related concepts but not interchangeable statuses.

  • Articles 5–11 primarily address citizenship at the commencement of the Constitution; Parliament regulates subsequent citizenship by law.

  • The Citizenship Act, 1955 provides statutory routes such as birth, descent, registration, naturalisation and incorporation of territory, subject to their conditions.

  • The Act also distinguishes renunciation, termination and deprivation.

  • India has single citizenship rather than a separate state citizenship.

  • Overseas Citizenship of India is not full dual citizenship and does not by itself confer voting rights.

  • Eligibility rules depend on dates and amendments; use the current consolidated Act and rules rather than treating this edition's account as current law.

Mains prompt: Differentiate citizenship as a legal status from constitutional protections available to all persons.

An OCI cardholder is, solely by virtue of that registration:
  1. Automatically entitled to vote in Lok Sabha elections
  2. A holder of full dual citizenship
  3. Not thereby granted Indian voting citizenship
  4. Automatically eligible to become President

Answer: Not thereby granted Indian voting citizenship

OCI is not full dual citizenship and does not itself confer political citizenship rights such as voting. Eligibility for constitutional offices cannot be inferred from OCI registration.

Fundamental Rights · मौलिक अधिकार

Fundamental Rights restrain public power and protect conditions for a life of dignity. To solve a question, identify the right-holder, the duty-bearer, the permitted restriction and the remedy before deciding whether a right has been violated.

  • Article 12 defines State for Part III; Article 13 deals with inconsistency between laws and Fundamental Rights.

  • Articles 14–18 address equality. Equality can require reasonable classification rather than identical treatment in every situation.

  • Article 19 protects specified freedoms of citizens; Article 21 protects life and personal liberty of persons.

  • Articles 23–24 address exploitation; Articles 25–28 religion; Articles 29–30 cultural and educational interests.

  • Article 32 itself is a Fundamental Right; Article 226 gives High Courts writ jurisdiction for Fundamental Rights and other legal purposes.

  • Property is protected under Article 300A, outside Part III; Articles 33–35 address special situations and legislative competence.

Expanded guide: A rights-analysis method

Begin by identifying the claimant. Articles 14 and 21 use the language of persons, while Article 19 protects citizens. Next identify the respondent: Article 12 includes named governmental bodies and other authorities whose status depends on legal tests. Some rights, such as those against untouchability and forced labour, also have horizontal implications. A private actor is therefore neither automatically outside all rights analysis nor automatically State for every purpose.

Separate deprivation from constitutional justification. A restriction on speech requires a legal basis and must fit the constitutionally permitted grounds and applicable standards. Administrative convenience alone is not an unlimited exception. Equality analysis asks whether a classification has an intelligible differentia and a rational relation to the objective, alongside the broader constitutional jurisprudence against arbitrariness. These tests should not be mechanically substituted for one another in every case.

Choose the remedy by the violated interest, jurisdiction and relief needed. Habeas corpus tests unlawful detention; mandamus directs performance of a public/legal duty in appropriate circumstances; prohibition restrains an inferior court or tribunal from exceeding jurisdiction; certiorari can quash a legally defective decision; quo warranto questions lawful authority to hold a public office. Their availability depends on conditions, not simply on a memorised translation.

Do not collapse all emergency effects into suspension of rights. Article 358 and Article 359 operate differently. Article 359 concerns the right to move courts for specified rights under the order, with Articles 20 and 21 excluded from that power. An examination statement that all remedies and all rights always disappear on a national emergency is therefore unsound.

Application: A district authority issues a blanket, indefinite order stopping every public meeting without identifying any specific risk. Examine the legal authority, the affected Article 19 freedoms, the permitted grounds, the connection between evidence and restriction, the breadth and duration of the order, and available judicial relief. Do not simply assert that public order makes every restriction valid.

Source-informed explanations

Source-informed original expansion · independent review pending · consulted 2026-09-19

1. Start with the purpose of a right

मौलिक अधिकार: सत्ता पर सीमा और व्यक्ति की सुरक्षा।

A right is not simply a benefit that a government may withdraw whenever it becomes inconvenient. A Fundamental Right has constitutional protection. It places limits on public power and gives the individual a route to challenge a violation. This is why a government elected by a large majority must still respect constitutional rights: winning an election gives authority to govern, not unlimited authority over people.

Think of two separate questions. First, what may the State do to a person? Second, what must the State do to protect people from exploitation or exclusion? Rights matter in both situations. A discriminatory government order is one problem; authorities ignoring forced labour is another. Good constitutional analysis examines the source of the injury and the duty of the public authority instead of assuming that every violation has the same legal form.

An original example: a district office refuses to accept an application solely because the applicant belongs to an unpopular community. The issue is not merely rude service. Ask which equality guarantee is involved, whether the office is a public authority, what evidence establishes discrimination and which remedy can stop it. A right becomes useful when its holder can identify a duty and seek an effective remedy.

Basis: NCERT: The importance of rights; Bill of Rights

2. A four-question method for any rights problem

किसका अधिकार, किसकी जिम्मेदारी, कौन-सी सीमा, क्या उपचार?

First identify the right-holder. Some guarantees protect persons generally, whereas specified freedoms protect citizens. Second identify the respondent and duty: government action, a legally recognised public duty, or a private act covered by a particular protection. Third identify the restriction. Do not assume that a restriction is lawful merely because an official says it serves the public interest. Fourth identify the remedy and the court or statutory authority able to grant it.

The word fundamental does not mean every right is absolute. Different provisions contain different conditions, and those conditions cannot be exchanged at will. A restriction on a religious practice and a restriction on a business activity must be tested against their respective constitutional rules. Equally, the existence of restrictions does not make rights meaningless: government still has to act within law and remains subject to judicial scrutiny.

Use this method before learning long lists of cases. It prevents a common Mains weakness: naming an Article without showing how the facts fit it. The detailed meaning of State under Article 12 and invalidity under Article 13 needs provision-by-provision and case-law study; this source-informed introductory method does not claim to exhaust either subject.

Basis: NCERT: Fundamental Rights in the Indian Constitution; Right to Constitutional Remedies

3. Equality does not always mean identical treatment

समानता का अर्थ हर परिस्थिति में बिल्कुल एक जैसा व्यवहार नहीं है।

Formal equality asks whether the same rule applies to everyone. Substantive equality asks whether social disadvantage prevents people from using the opportunity in practice. A building may announce that everyone can enter, but a staircase-only entrance still excludes some persons with disabilities. Removing that barrier is not an attack on equality; it can be a way to make equal access real.

Distinguish the equality ideas rather than treating Articles 14 to 18 as a single slogan. Equality before law and equal protection address legal treatment. Non-discrimination and access provisions address specified forms of exclusion. Equality in public employment concerns access to government service. Abolition of untouchability confronts a particular system of social exclusion. Abolition of titles serves the rejection of artificial civic hierarchy, subject to the constitutional treatment of military and academic distinctions.

Reservations and other special measures must be studied within the specific constitutional provisions that permit them. They are not proof that equality has been abandoned, nor does every policy called affirmative action automatically satisfy all legal requirements. In an answer, explain the disadvantage being addressed, the legal basis, the design of the measure and the need for review. Avoid inventing a universal quota rule that applies to every institution and category.

Basis: NCERT: Right to Equality

4. Freedom: read the guarantee and its limits together

स्वतंत्रता के साथ उसकी संवैधानिक सीमाएँ भी पढ़ें।

Freedom enables people to speak, organise, move, choose livelihoods and participate in public life. Article 19 protects specified freedoms of citizens. For revision, connect each freedom to a real activity: speaking at a public meeting, forming an association, moving to another state, settling there or running a lawful business. This makes it easier to recognise questions in which several freedoms are affected by the same order.

A restriction is not justified simply because somebody dislikes a speech or protest. Conversely, calling an activity an exercise of freedom does not immunise it from every lawful restriction. The correct sequence is to identify the exact freedom, the legal basis for the restriction, the constitutionally relevant ground and whether the measure is defensible under the applicable standard. Read exact grounds from the Article rather than treating all restrictions as a general public-interest clause.

Original application: a peaceful procession is rerouted because a bridge is structurally unsafe. Compare a short, evidence-based rerouting with an indefinite ban on all meetings across a district. Both restrict an activity, but their reasons, geographical reach, duration and available alternatives are different. In Mains, this comparison is more useful than writing either 'all bans are unconstitutional' or 'public order permits every ban'.

Basis: NCERT: Right to Freedom; Other freedoms

5. Life, liberty and the position of an accused person

आरोप लगना दोष सिद्ध होना नहीं है।

Life and personal liberty concern more than mere biological survival. NCERT explains the judicial expansion of the right towards dignity and conditions necessary for meaningful life. This does not mean every desirable public service is automatically available as an unconditional individual entitlement. The wording of the guarantee, the relevant judgment, the governing law and the relief sought still matter.

An accusation must not be treated as a conviction. Procedural safeguards are especially important when a person faces the coercive power of the State. The protections concerning retrospective criminal punishment, repeated prosecution and punishment for the same offence, and compelled self-incrimination address different risks. Do not turn the first into a claim that every retrospective civil or tax law is prohibited; do not turn the last into a claim that every form of evidence collection is forbidden.

For ordinary arrest, learn the information, legal-representation and production-before-a-magistrate safeguards, including their constitutional qualifications. The 24-hour rule excludes necessary journey time. Preventive detention is a distinct constitutional category with its own safeguards and exceptions. A concise textbook summary is not enough to resolve its exact time limits in every statutory situation. For an exam statement, return to the applicable Article and current detention law rather than generalising from an ordinary criminal arrest.

Basis: NCERT: Right to life and personal liberty; Rights of accused

6. Exploitation: constitutional protection also matters outside government offices

शोषण के विरुद्ध अधिकार निजी व्यक्तियों के आचरण से भी जुड़ते हैं।

Exploitation can involve trafficking, forced labour and prohibited child employment. The central idea is that poverty or social dependence must not become a licence to treat a human being as an instrument. A worker may appear to agree to a condition while having little meaningful choice because of debt, threats or extreme vulnerability. Constitutional analysis therefore cannot stop at the claim that a contract was signed.

Articles 23 and 24 should be distinguished. One addresses trafficking and forced labour; the other addresses employment of children below fourteen in factories, mines and other hazardous employment. Statutory child-labour protections go beyond a short constitutional heading and must be read separately. Do not infer that every activity outside the exact words of Article 24 is therefore lawful.

Original application: a brick-kiln worker is told that an old debt prevents the family from leaving employment. Identify the coercion, the vulnerable persons, the public authority responsible for enforcement and the evidence required. In a Mains answer, legal prohibition is only the beginning: inspections, rescue, rehabilitation, schooling and access to alternative livelihoods determine whether the protection works.

Basis: NCERT: Right against Exploitation; The importance of rights

7. Religion: conscience, practice and equal citizenship

धर्म की स्वतंत्रता में किसी धर्म को न मानने की स्वतंत्रता भी शामिल है।

Freedom of conscience protects personal belief, including the choice not to follow a religion. Profession, practice and propagation are related but distinct activities. A person may state a belief, perform a religious practice or explain it to others. None of these expressions should be confused with a constitutional permission to force another person to accept a faith.

Religious freedom is subject to the relevant constitutional limitations, including public order, morality and health, and to other applicable provisions. A useful distinction is between protecting belief and examining the legal regulation of an activity associated with religion. A practice does not escape every law merely because it has a religious label. At the same time, administrative dislike of a community is not a legitimate substitute for a lawful justification.

Articles 25 to 28 cover more than individual worship: they also concern religious affairs, particular taxation issues and religious instruction or worship in specified educational institutions. The constitutional categories of institutions matter. Do not replace them with the sweeping statement that all religious teaching in every school is prohibited. For Mains, connect secularism to equal citizenship and freedom of conscience rather than reducing it to hostility towards religion.

Basis: NCERT: Right to Freedom of Religion; Freedom of faith and worship; Equality of all religions

8. Culture and education: preserving diversity without abandoning equality

भाषा और संस्कृति का संरक्षण लोकतांत्रिक विविधता को मजबूत करता है।

A democracy can use majority decision-making without requiring minorities to erase their identity. Cultural and educational protections make that distinction meaningful. They protect spaces in which language, script, culture and institutions can continue across generations, while the wider constitutional order continues to apply.

Read Articles 29 and 30 separately. Article 29's protection of distinct language, script or culture is not expressed as a right only for minorities; its admission-related provision also has its own wording. Article 30 specifically addresses religious and linguistic minorities establishing and administering educational institutions. The phrase cultural and educational rights is a convenient chapter label, not a reason to merge the holders and conditions of the two Articles.

Original application: when discussing a linguistic minority's school, separate the right to establish and administer the institution from questions about recognition, educational standards, aid and admissions. The actual legal outcome depends on the institution and applicable law. A good answer recognises both preservation of identity and legitimate regulation, instead of assuming either complete government control or complete immunity from standards.

Basis: NCERT: Cultural and Educational Rights

9. Remedies: a written promise needs an enforcement route

उपचार के बिना अधिकार का व्यावहारिक मूल्य कम हो जाता है।

Constitutional remedies connect a guarantee to a court capable of enforcing it. Article 32 concerns moving the Supreme Court for enforcement of Fundamental Rights. Article 226 empowers High Courts to issue writs for Fundamental Rights and for other legal purposes. The High Court's subject-matter reach is therefore broader, although jurisdiction and procedural considerations continue to apply.

Choose relief by asking what has gone wrong. Is a person unlawfully detained? Is a public authority failing to perform a duty? Has a tribunal acted outside its jurisdiction? Is somebody occupying a public office without the legal qualification? The same factual story may involve more than one legal issue, but a writ is not a magic word that bypasses all requirements.

An institutional remedy is different from social effectiveness. Filing costs, language, delay, lack of documents, fear of retaliation and weak compliance can prevent people from benefiting from a formal right. This is why legal aid, accessible administration and monitoring of compliance belong in a Mains discussion. Explain the constitutional route first, then explain what makes it work for a vulnerable claimant.

Basis: NCERT: Right to Constitutional Remedies

10. Understand the five writs by the problem they address

बंदी प्रत्यक्षीकरण, परमादेश, प्रतिषेध, उत्प्रेषण और अधिकार-पृच्छा।

Habeas corpus addresses unlawful detention. Its purpose is not to decide every aspect of the underlying criminal allegation; it tests the lawfulness of custody. Mandamus concerns performance of a public or legal duty in appropriate circumstances. The applicant must identify an actual duty, not merely a desirable action they would like the authority to take.

Prohibition restrains a lower court or tribunal from proceeding beyond lawful jurisdiction. Certiorari can quash a decision affected by the relevant jurisdictional or legal defect. For a first comparison, think prevention versus correction, but do not assume that this memory aid captures every procedural qualification. The exact grounds and availability depend on the governing law and judicial doctrine.

Quo warranto questions the lawful authority by which a person holds a public office. It is not a general device for challenging every private employment appointment. In a practice question, identify the nature of the office and the legal requirement allegedly breached. The common trap across all writs is memorising a translation while ignoring the claimant, respondent, legal defect and relief.

Basis: NCERT: Right to Constitutional Remedies; writ descriptions (introductory basis, with legal distinctions requiring case-law study)

11. Property, duties and rights outside Part III

भाग III के बाहर का संवैधानिक अधिकार भी महत्वहीन नहीं होता।

The right to property is no longer a Fundamental Right in Part III; Article 300A provides constitutional protection against deprivation except by authority of law. 'Not fundamental' does not mean 'not protected'. Its present status changes the constitutional route of analysis and remedy, but does not give officials an unrestricted power to take property.

Keep three categories distinct: a Fundamental Right, another constitutional right, and a right created by ordinary legislation. Their source, amendment requirements and enforcement routes differ. It is misleading to call every important legal entitlement a Fundamental Right, just as it is misleading to dismiss a statutory entitlement as optional.

Fundamental Duties encourage civic conduct, but enjoyment of Fundamental Rights is not generally a reward available only after an official certifies that duties have been performed. Laws may give effect to particular duties within constitutional limits. In an answer, show how rights, duties and public welfare can support one another without inventing a rule that automatically cancels an individual's rights for being an imperfect citizen.

Basis: NCERT: Right to Property; Fundamental Duties of citizens

12. Evaluate the system, not just the list

अधिकारों की सफलता उनका वास्तविक उपयोग कर पाने में है।

The achievement of a bill of rights is that it places some basic claims beyond ordinary political convenience. It protects dissent, legal equality, personal autonomy, diversity and access to remedies. Its weaknesses in practice may include delay, uneven awareness, social pressure and the difficulty of securing compliance. These are reasons to strengthen institutions, not evidence that constitutional guarantees have no value.

For a 150-word answer, use four moves: explain the constitutional purpose, identify the relevant guarantee, demonstrate an implementation difficulty and propose a specific institutional improvement. A proposal such as accessible legal aid is stronger when you identify who needs it and what barrier it removes. Avoid ending every answer with an unexplained demand for awareness or strict implementation.

Scope boundary: these twelve sections develop the main rights groups and their use. They do not exhaust the source photograph's separate headings on Articles 12–13, Articles 31A–31C, armed forces, martial law, legislative competence or emergency effects. Those headings remain visible in the coverage register and require further provision-level research. The original book's Notes and References pages have not been supplied.

Basis: NCERT: The importance of rights; Conclusion

Exam trap: Not every Fundamental Right is restricted to citizens, and not every right operates only against the State.

Mains prompt: How do constitutional remedies convert formal rights into practical protection?

Consider: 1. Article 19 freedoms are available to citizens. 2. Article 21 protects persons, not only citizens. Which is correct?
  1. 1 only
  2. 2 only
  3. Both 1 and 2
  4. Neither

Answer: Both 1 and 2

Both are correct. Different Fundamental Rights have different right-holders; it is unsafe to describe all Part III rights as citizen-only.

Which comparison of writ powers is accurate?
  1. Article 32 extends to all ordinary contractual disputes automatically
  2. Article 226 can address Fundamental Rights and other legal purposes
  3. Only the Supreme Court can issue habeas corpus
  4. Article 226 is itself located in Part III

Answer: Article 226 can address Fundamental Rights and other legal purposes

Article 226 permits High Court writs for Fundamental Rights and other legal purposes, within applicable limits. Article 32 addresses enforcement of Fundamental Rights; High Courts can also issue habeas corpus; Article 226 is outside Part III.

Directive Principles of State Policy · राज्य के नीति निदेशक तत्त्व

Directive Principles guide the use of state power toward social and economic justice. They are not directly enforceable by courts, but their non-justiciability does not make them constitutionally insignificant.

  • Part IV contains Articles 36–51; Article 37 declares the principles fundamental in governance while excluding direct judicial enforceability.

  • Article 39 addresses distribution and welfare objectives; Article 39A links justice with free legal aid.

  • Article 40 concerns village panchayats; Article 44 a uniform civil code; Article 48A environmental protection.

  • Classifications into socialist, Gandhian and liberal-intellectual principles are analytical groupings, not constitutional headings.

  • Article 45 was changed by the 86th Amendment; distinguish its early-childhood focus from the Article 21A right.

  • Minerva Mills (1980) emphasised harmony between Parts III and IV and limited amending power.

Source-informed explanations

Source-informed original expansion · independent review pending · consulted 2026-09-19

1. Why a Constitution contains policy directions

नीति निदेशक तत्व शासन को सामाजिक न्याय की दिशा देते हैं।

Political democracy is incomplete if many people cannot obtain education, basic nutrition, health care or a reasonable livelihood. Directive Principles express a constitutional direction towards social and economic transformation. They help answer not only who may govern, but what public purposes governance should pursue. They are not simply a list of programmes announced by one political party.

Their non-justiciability means that they are not, by themselves, enforceable in court in the same manner as Fundamental Rights. It does not mean that they are irrelevant, unconstitutional or optional decorations. They inform legislation, political accountability and constitutional interpretation. A law implementing a directive may create specific enforceable statutory entitlements; the enforceability then needs to be examined through that law and the wider constitutional framework.

Basis: NCERT: Directive Principles of State Policy

2. Read goals, policy directions and implementation separately

लक्ष्य, नीति और परिणाम तीन अलग प्रश्न हैं।

Some directives concern broad goals such as welfare, justice and reduced inequality. Others indicate policy directions, such as village self-government or particular social reforms. A third way to read them is through people's material needs, including livelihood, education and humane working conditions. These categories help understanding; familiar coaching labels such as socialist, Gandhian and liberal-intellectual are analytical groupings, not headings written into the Constitution.

Original example: to evaluate a nutrition programme, distinguish the constitutional goal of improved well-being, the statutory or administrative scheme chosen, the budget allocated and the actual service delivered. A budget announcement is not proof that nutrition improved. Likewise, a disappointing outcome does not alone establish that the constitutional goal was legally enforceable in the exact form demanded. Connect law, finance, administration and evidence.

Basis: NCERT: What do the Directive Principles contain?

3. Rights and directives: avoid a false either-or

व्यक्तिगत स्वतंत्रता और सामाजिक न्याय को साथ पढ़ें।

Rights protect individuals against certain exercises of power, while directives guide the State towards a more just social order. This is a useful starting contrast, not an absolute division: some rights require positive State action and social policy can help people use their freedoms. A child who receives an education gains more meaningful opportunity to participate in public life.

Tension arises when a redistributive or regulatory measure affects protected interests. The answer is not that every welfare objective automatically overrides every right. Nor is it that rights prevent all social reform. Constitutional amendments, legislation and judicial interpretation shape the relationship, subject to constitutional limits. The exact scope of Article 31C and the relevant basic-structure decisions needs separate case-law verification; an introductory NCERT discussion does not replace those judgments.

Basis: NCERT: Relationship between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles

4. Build an evaluative Mains answer

घोषणा से आगे बढ़कर संस्थाएँ, संसाधन और जवाबदेही देखें।

A strong answer can connect a directive to an implementation chain: constitutional objective, law or scheme, funding, responsible institution, accessible delivery and measurable outcome. For decentralisation, for example, creating an elected body is only one step; functions, finances and staff determine whether it can act. For labour welfare, a rule without inspection or an accessible complaint mechanism may leave workers unprotected.

An original answer plan for 'Are non-justiciable directives still important?' is: explain their status; show how they guide legislation and evaluation of government; acknowledge resource constraints and the absence of a direct remedy based solely on a directive; conclude that constitutional significance is broader than immediate enforceability. Do not substitute a long list of Article numbers for that reasoning.

Basis: NCERT: Directive Principles; original application

Mains prompt: Discuss why enforceable liberties and non-justiciable social goals must be read together.

Directive Principles are:
  1. Directly enforceable in exactly the same way as all Fundamental Rights
  2. Not directly enforceable by courts, but fundamental in governance

Article 37 distinguishes non-justiciability from constitutional importance. Directive Principles are constitutional, not executive circulars, and do not automatically override all rights.

Fundamental Duties · मौलिक कर्तव्य

Fundamental Duties express civic responsibilities that support a constitutional community. Analyse duties alongside rights: they guide conduct and interpretation but cannot become a general excuse to disregard legal safeguards.

  • Article 51A in Part IVA lists citizens' duties.

  • Ten duties were inserted by the 42nd Amendment; the 86th Amendment added the educational duty of parents or guardians concerning children aged six to fourteen.

  • Duties include respecting constitutional ideals, promoting harmony, protecting the environment and developing scientific temper.

  • The Swaran Singh Committee is associated with their inclusion; the Verma Committee examined ways of giving them effect.

  • Duties are not directly enforced by a writ merely because they appear in Article 51A; valid legislation can create enforceable obligations.

Amendment of the Constitution · संविधान संशोधन

Constitutional amendment allows change without abandoning constitutional continuity. The difficulty of amendment varies with what is being altered, so classify a proposal by its legal route before counting votes.

  • Article 368 sets out a special amendment procedure and constituent power.

  • The usual special majority is a majority of the total membership of each House plus at least two-thirds of members present and voting.

  • Specified federal provisions also require ratification by legislatures of at least half the states.

  • An amendment bill may originate in either House; there is no joint sitting to resolve disagreement on it.

  • Some constitutional changes are made by ordinary legislative procedures and are not amendments for Article 368 purposes.

  • All Article 368 amendments remain subject to the basic-structure limitation.

Exam trap: Two-thirds of those present and voting alone does not satisfy Article 368 if a majority of total membership is absent.

Mains prompt: Evaluate whether India's amendment system balances flexibility, federalism and constitutional stability.

An Article 368 amendment requiring no state ratification still generally needs:
  1. Only a majority of members present and voting
  2. A majority of total membership and two-thirds of those present and voting in each House
  3. Only Rajya Sabha approval
  4. A joint sitting in every case

Answer: A majority of total membership and two-thirds of those present and voting in each House

The special majority has two limbs and must be met separately in each House. Joint sitting is not a route for constitutional amendment bills.

Basic Structure of the Constitution · संविधान का मूल ढाँचा

The basic-structure doctrine limits Parliament's power to alter the Constitution. Its purpose is to distinguish legitimate constitutional change from destruction of the constitutional order that authorises the change.

  • Kesavananda Bharati (1973) held that the amending power does not extend to damaging the basic structure.

  • The doctrine primarily tests constitutional amendments, not every ordinary statute in the same manner.

  • Judicial review, constitutional supremacy and limited amending power are among recognised elements.

  • The elements have emerged through cases rather than an exhaustive list enacted in the Constitution.

  • Minerva Mills (1980) reaffirmed limited amending power; I. R. Coelho (2007) addressed Ninth Schedule protection after 24 April 1973.

Mains prompt: Is the basic-structure doctrine a protection of democracy or a constraint upon elected authority? Discuss both sides.

The basic-structure doctrine principally limits:
  1. Only municipal taxation
  2. Parliament’s constitutional amending power
  3. All political debate
  4. Only the President’s election

Answer: Parliament’s constitutional amending power

The doctrine limits constitutional amendment so that the foundational constitutional order is not destroyed. It is not a ban on debate or a rule confined to one office.

Polity · ORIGINAL CORE LESSON · SOURCE REVIEW PENDING

Parliamentary System · संसदीय प्रणाली

A parliamentary system makes the political executive responsible to the legislature, especially its confidence chamber. The distinction from a presidential system concerns the source and continuity of executive authority, not the existence of a President as such.

  • India's President is the constitutional head, while the Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister normally exercises political executive authority.

  • Collective responsibility to Lok Sabha under Article 75 is central to the Union system.

  • A minister who is not a member of Parliament must secure membership within six months to continue.

  • A presidential system typically has a separately elected executive with a fixed tenure, subject to constitutional removal mechanisms.

  • India has a written supreme Constitution and judicial review; British parliamentary sovereignty cannot simply be transplanted to India.

Federal System · संघीय प्रणाली

Federalism distributes public power territorially and protects more than one level of government. Indian federalism combines constitutionally allocated authority with mechanisms for cooperation and, in specified circumstances, a stronger Union role.

  • The Seventh Schedule distributes legislative subjects through Union, State and Concurrent Lists.

  • A written Constitution, division of powers and independent adjudication are important federal features.

  • Residuary legislative powers are vested in Parliament under Article 248, read with the relevant list entry.

  • Single citizenship, an integrated judiciary and emergency arrangements are among centralising features.

  • States are not mere administrative departments: their constitutionally assigned sphere is protected by constitutional supremacy.

  • Asymmetrical arrangements recognise that some territories or groups require differentiated institutional protection.

Source-informed explanations

Source-informed original expansion · independent review pending · consulted 2026-09-19

1. Federalism shares power, not merely administrative work

संघवाद में क्षेत्रीय सरकार की शक्ति का संवैधानिक आधार होता है।

A large organisation may delegate work to a local office and later withdraw it. Federalism is different: the regional government's authority has a constitutional basis rather than depending entirely on the convenience of a superior administrator. Both national and state governments have defined spheres, and disputes about their powers need a constitutional method of settlement.

India combines common national membership with strong regional identities. Being attached to a language or a state need not conflict with belonging to the Union. Federal institutions allow different communities to participate in shared rule while exercising self-government in designated areas. The value of federalism therefore lies not only in administrative efficiency but also in recognition, representation and the accommodation of diversity.

Basis: NCERT: What is Federalism?

2. The lists are a map of responsibility

संघ सूची, राज्य सूची और समवर्ती सूची को उदाहरणों से समझें।

Defence and currency call for national coordination. Police, agriculture and many local services involve substantial state responsibility. Subjects such as education and forests appear in the Concurrent List, where both levels can legislate within the constitutional scheme. These examples help explain the lists, but the full legal entry must be read when a dispute concerns overlapping subject matter.

The label of a ministry or the political popularity of an issue does not decide legislative competence. A question may require examining the real nature of a law and its relation to several entries. Residuary authority addresses matters not assigned in the lists; it is not a licence to ignore a subject already covered by a specific entry. Learn the structure before attempting difficult competence and repugnancy problems.

Basis: NCERT: Federalism in the Indian Constitution; Division of Powers

3. A strong Union and meaningful states can coexist

मजबूत केंद्र का अर्थ राज्यों का संवैधानिक अस्तित्व समाप्त होना नहीं है।

The constitutional design responded to integration, national security, development and the risk of fragmentation. It therefore gives the Union important advantages, including significant fiscal capacity and powers in specified exceptional situations. These features explain the description of a federal system with a centralising tendency; they do not erase elected state governments or all limits on Union action.

Distinguish a normal division of powers from an exceptional constitutional route. A special parliamentary power over a state subject has a trigger, procedure and scope. Simply listing emergency provisions without explaining those conditions produces the mistaken impression that the Union can always do anything. Equally, describing India as federal does not mean every state has an absolute veto over every national decision.

Basis: NCERT: Federalism with a Strong Central Government

4. Trust is part of how institutions work

सहयोग केवल एक शब्द नहीं, नियमित परामर्श और भरोसे की प्रक्रिया है।

A written division of powers cannot anticipate every policy problem. Floods, epidemics, migration, transport networks and environmental damage cross state borders. Effective federalism requires shared information, predictable finance, consultation and a willingness to resolve disagreements without treating every dispute as disloyalty.

For Mains, evaluate both cooperation and legitimate disagreement. A state can question a funding formula while still participating in a common programme. Competition can encourage better delivery, but it may also disadvantage states with weak starting capacity unless supported by fair transfers. Avoid writing that competitive and cooperative federalism are necessarily opposites; ask what institutional design makes each productive.

Basis: NCERT: What is Federalism?; Conflicts in India's Federal System

Centre–State Relations · केंद्र–राज्य संबंध

Centre–state relations operate through legislative competence, administrative coordination and fiscal transfers. A sound answer separates legal allocation from the practical balance of revenue, personnel and political bargaining.

  • Articles 245–255 deal broadly with legislative relations and Articles 256–263 with administrative relations.

  • Article 254 addresses repugnancy concerning Concurrent List laws; it is not a blanket rule for every conflict.

  • Parliament may legislate on state subjects through specific constitutional routes, including Articles 249, 250, 252 and 253.

  • Tax powers, Finance Commission recommendations, grants and borrowing shape fiscal relations.

  • All India Services and intergovernmental institutions link administration across levels.

  • Sarkaria and Punchhi Commission recommendations are analytical resources, not automatically binding constitutional rules.

Printed source checklist · book pp. 14.1–14.25
  • Legislative Relations — 14.1 · full expansion pending
  • Administrative Relations — 14.5 · full expansion pending
  • Financial Relations — 14.9 · full expansion pending
  • Trends in Centre–State Relations — 14.16 · full expansion pending
  • Notes and References — 14.24 · full expansion pending
Expanded guide: From lists to real federal bargaining

Classify the dispute first. Legislative competence asks which legislature can enact the law. Repugnancy concerns incompatibility in the relevant Concurrent List setting and is not the starting rule for every difference between state and Union policy. Administrative compliance involves implementation obligations and lawful directions. Fiscal conflict involves tax assignment, transfers, grants or borrowing. Mixing these categories produces vague answers.

For an exceptional parliamentary law on a state subject, identify the constitutional gateway. Article 249 involves the prescribed Rajya Sabha resolution in the national interest; Article 250 operates during a national emergency; Article 252 concerns consenting states and a specific parliamentary route; Article 253 addresses implementation of international obligations. The triggers, duration and capacity to alter resulting laws differ. They are not interchangeable evidence that the State List has no protection.

Fiscal capacity determines how meaningful formal autonomy can be. A state may have substantial service-delivery obligations while its own-source revenues are insufficient. Transfers address that gap, but their predictability, conditions and formula also affect incentives and policy space. Distinguish Finance Commission recommendations, GST arrangements, specific grants and borrowing constraints before proposing a reform.

Application: A new national service standard places substantial costs on states. Assess consultation, legal competence, costing, predictable finance, reporting burden and scope for state adaptation. Central funding without local implementation capacity may still fail; state autonomy without accountability is not a sufficient solution either.

Source-informed explanations

Source-informed original expansion · independent review pending · consulted 2026-09-19

1. Separate legislative, administrative and financial relations

कानून बनाने, लागू करने और खर्च उठाने की समस्याएँ अलग हो सकती हैं।

A Centre–State dispute is easier to understand once it is classified. Legislative relations concern the authority to make a law. Administrative relations concern implementation, coordination and lawful directions. Financial relations concern the assignment of revenue, transfers, expenditure and borrowing. A dispute may involve more than one category, but the categories require different evidence and remedies.

Original example: a state wants to improve district hospitals. The authority to administer the service, eligibility for a centrally supported grant, recruitment of staff and the terms of borrowing are not one question. An answer that merely demands more autonomy misses the mechanism. Identify the particular constraint, then assess a proposal to change it.

Basis: NCERT: Division of Powers; Demands for Autonomy

2. Financial autonomy gives practical meaning to responsibility

जिम्मेदारी के साथ पर्याप्त और पूर्वानुमेय संसाधन भी चाहिए।

States deliver many visible public services while important revenue sources are concentrated at the Union level. Transfers can help bridge this mismatch and address differences in states' fiscal capacity and needs. Their design matters: an unpredictable transfer makes planning difficult, while a very tightly conditioned transfer may leave little room for local priorities.

Separate a state's own revenue from its share of common taxes, grants and borrowing. Borrowing is financing that creates future obligations; it is not the same as a permanent increase in revenue. Similarly, do not assume every transfer is an identical discretionary grant. For contemporary answers, verify the applicable Finance Commission period, budget documents and legal arrangements rather than reproducing an old formula from memory.

Basis: NCERT: Division of Powers; Federalism with a Strong Central Government; Demands for Autonomy

3. Autonomy has several meanings

स्वायत्तता राजनीतिक, वित्तीय, प्रशासनिक और सांस्कृतिक हो सकती है।

A demand for autonomy may seek a change in legislative responsibilities, greater control over funds, less interference in administration or protection for language and culture. These demands should not all be interpreted as demands for separation. Federal politics often concerns the terms of working together within the Union.

Party competition affects how constitutional arrangements are used, but party labels are not constitutional arguments. Ask whether consultation took place, whether reasons were publicly explained and whether the same principle would be acceptable if the parties in office were reversed. That is a useful test of institutional fairness in questions about governors, grants and the administration of joint schemes.

Basis: NCERT: Centre-State Relations; Demands for Autonomy

4. Use history without freezing the present

पुराने संस्थागत उदाहरण को वर्तमान व्यवस्था न मानें।

The consulted NCERT chapter discusses the Planning Commission as part of the history of centralised development planning. That discussion must not be copied as a statement about the present institutional arrangement. Likewise, a textbook's account of a period of single-party dominance or coalition government illustrates political change; it is not a permanent rule about every future election.

A balanced reform answer links each problem to a remedy: predictable transfers for planning uncertainty, consultation before common programme design, transparent reasons in contested decisions, better dispute-resolution forums and greater administrative capacity. Identify which proposal changes the Constitution, which changes a statute and which can be achieved through routine institutional practice.

Basis: NCERT: historical discussion of Centre-State relations; source limitation

Inter-State Relations · अंतर्राज्यीय संबंध

States share rivers, markets, people and infrastructure. The Constitution therefore creates channels for coordination and dispute resolution instead of assuming that territorial allocation alone prevents conflict.

  • Article 262 permits parliamentary provision for adjudication of inter-state river-water disputes and exclusion of specified court jurisdiction.

  • Article 263 concerns an Inter-State Council for inquiry, discussion and coordination when established under its terms.

  • Article 261 concerns public acts, records and judicial proceedings.

  • Articles 301–307 address freedom of trade, commerce and intercourse subject to constitutional qualifications.

  • Zonal Councils arise from legislation, not Article 263; the North Eastern Council has a separate statutory basis.

  • Political negotiation and technical assessment remain important alongside legal adjudication.

Emergency Provisions · आपातकालीन प्रावधान

Emergency provisions permit exceptional constitutional responses to specified crises. They must be studied through their triggers, approvals, duration, effects and safeguards—not as a single unlimited suspension of the Constitution.

  • Article 352 concerns war, external aggression or armed rebellion; the 44th Amendment replaced the earlier internal-disturbance wording.

  • Article 356 concerns failure of constitutional machinery in a state; Article 360 concerns financial emergency.

  • Article 358's effect on Article 19 is confined to a national emergency grounded in war or external aggression.

  • Under Article 359, an order concerning court enforcement cannot cover Articles 20 and 21.

  • A proclamation under Article 356 is judicially reviewable; S. R. Bommai (1994) is central to the safeguards.

  • Different emergencies have different approval and continuation rules; do not transfer a rule from one Article to another.

President · राष्ट्रपति

The President is the constitutional head of the Union and an integral constituent of Parliament. Formal powers must be read with the parliamentary requirement of ministerial advice and the Constitution's specific exceptions or processes.

  • The electoral college includes elected members of both Houses and elected members of state assemblies, including constitutionally specified Union territories.

  • Proportional representation by the single transferable vote and a secret ballot are prescribed.

  • Article 74 requires aid and advice; the President may require reconsideration but must act on advice tendered after reconsideration.

  • Article 111 governs assent to bills; a non-Money Bill may be returned once under its terms.

  • Article 123 permits ordinances when both Houses are not simultaneously in session and immediate action is necessary.

  • Article 72 includes clemency in specified cases, including all death sentences.

Vice-President · उपराष्ट्रपति

The Vice-President bridges executive succession and parliamentary presiding functions. Study the office separately from the President because the electorates, eligibility requirements and removal procedures differ.

  • Members of both Houses, including nominated members, elect the Vice-President; state assemblies do not participate.

  • The Vice-President is ex officio Chairman of Rajya Sabha.

  • Eligibility includes qualification for election as a member of Rajya Sabha.

  • Removal begins with a Rajya Sabha resolution meeting the constitutional majority, agreed to by Lok Sabha, with the required notice.

  • When acting as President, the Vice-President does not perform the Chairman's duties during that period.

Prime Minister · प्रधानमंत्री

The Prime Minister is the principal coordinator of the Union political executive. Appointment is formally by the President, but the ability to command Lok Sabha's confidence is the essential democratic foundation.

  • Article 75 provides for appointment by the President; other ministers are appointed on the Prime Minister's advice.

  • Article 78 concerns communication of decisions and information to the President.

  • The Prime Minister coordinates ministries, leads the Council of Ministers and influences the legislative agenda.

  • A coalition requires negotiation within the executive as well as maintenance of legislative confidence.

  • Resignation or death of the Prime Minister has consequences for the Council of Ministers as a body.

Central Council of Ministers · केंद्रीय मंत्रिपरिषद

The Council of Ministers translates electoral responsibility into executive action. The Cabinet is its leading decision-making component, but constitutional responsibility attaches to the wider Council.

  • Articles 74 and 75 are the main constitutional anchors.

  • The Council is collectively responsible to Lok Sabha; a no-confidence defeat concerns the ministry as a whole.

  • Ministers hold office during the President's pleasure in the context of the parliamentary system.

  • The 91st Amendment limits the Union Council, including the Prime Minister, to 15% of Lok Sabha's total strength.

  • Cabinet ministers, ministers of state and deputy ministers are conventional categories rather than a full hierarchy specified in Article 75.

  • An informal kitchen cabinet has no independent constitutional decision-making authority.

Cabinet Committees · मंत्रिमंडलीय समितियाँ

Cabinet committees divide complex executive business among smaller groups while preserving coordination. They are mechanisms of government procedure, not substitutes for Parliament's legislative or financial authorisation.

  • They are extra-constitutional in the sense that their detailed organisation is not prescribed in the constitutional text.

  • Business rules under Article 77 support executive transaction and allocation of work.

  • Committees can be standing or ad hoc and may handle appointments, security, economic affairs or parliamentary coordination.

  • Their membership and subjects can change with government decisions.

  • Groups of Ministers are executive coordination arrangements and must not be confused with parliamentary committees.

Parliament · संसद

Parliament combines law-making, executive scrutiny, representation and authorisation of public finance. Its power is constitutionally limited, unlike an unlimited claim of parliamentary sovereignty.

  • Article 79 includes the President, Rajya Sabha and Lok Sabha.

  • Rajya Sabha is a continuing chamber; Lok Sabha is subject to dissolution. Both normally require six months or less between the last sitting of one session and the first of the next.

  • Article 108 provides a joint sitting for specified legislative deadlocks, not Money Bills or constitutional amendment bills.

  • Article 110 defines Money Bills. Rajya Sabha's role is recommendatory and time-limited for such bills.

  • The annual financial statement under Article 112 is accompanied by distinct demands, appropriation and taxation procedures.

  • Question Hour, motions, debates and committee work scrutinise the executive; disruption can weaken these mechanisms.

  • Article 105 privileges protect legislative functioning but do not place every act of a member beyond judicial scrutiny.
